messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Pharmacist
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water, Arguments: Arguments, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Avoid Similar People: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar, Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amina is a 20-year-old African woman who has been working as a pharmacist while trying to keep up with her relationship and her family’s expectations, but she now moves through her days as if the world has become a place of hidden ambushes. Her difficulties began after she was held and tortured during a period of political unrest, when she was forced to lie on the ground and had her body controlled against her will while she believed she might not survive. She does not tell the story easily; when she tries, the account fragments into pieces, and she says she can only remember flashes of hands, pressure, pain, and the hard surface beneath her. What remains most vividly is bodily: when the memory comes, she feels as though her own body is back in that position, pinned and helpless, while the rest stays incomplete and missing, almost impossible to put into words.

Since then, certain moments have become especially potent. Water, flooding, and large bodies of water unsettle her immediately, and so do arguments or any situation in which she feels forced to do something. A loud disagreement near her apartment building, a sink running too long, or seeing floodwater pooling in the street can bring back the same helpless bodily sensation and a rush of alarm. In those moments she becomes convinced that she must always be on guard, that she cannot afford to let her attention drift, and she thinks that if she even begins to remember the event in full she will not be able to handle it. She also feels guilty for surviving when others did not, and at times tells herself she deserves to suffer because of what happened. The combination leaves her feeling both frightened and morally condemned, as though danger and punishment are somehow still waiting for her.

That belief has shaped the way Amina moves through everyday life. She constantly scans her surroundings for signs of danger and identifies escape routes before she feels comfortable anywhere, whether she is entering the pharmacy where she works, sitting in a café with her partner, or arriving at a new building. If she is scheduled to close the pharmacy, she checks the back exit and the route to the parking lot before she can settle at the counter. At night she has difficulty falling asleep because she needs to stay alert, and she arranges her evening around avoiding the kinds of hours or situations that bring on nightmares. She also avoids seeing people who were involved in the event or who look similar to them, and even brief encounters with strangers who resemble those men can leave her tense and searching for a way out. These habits have narrowed her world, but she experiences them as necessary precautions rather than choices.

The more Amina tries to keep herself safe, the more the memory stays active. Scanning every room and mapping exits keeps her body braced in the same frozen posture, and the effort of staying alert makes the fragments of the torture return in sharper bodily form. Avoiding anything that might bring on dreams has not erased them; it has made sleep feel like another dangerous threshold, so that nights are organized around fear rather than rest. Her vigilance also feeds the very triggers she dreads, because arguments feel more explosive when she is already keyed up, and any sense of being cornered or forced intensifies her reactions. She has become more certain that she must be on guard all the time, and that certainty has deepened her conviction that she will not be able to bear what comes back to mind.

Over time, Amina has come to believe that thinking about the event itself is unsafe, so she pushes the memories away and treats them as if they were intolerable. Yet the more she avoids them, the less complete they feel, and the gaps in the story trouble her further; she is left with a disjointed bodily recollection that seems to prove something terrible happened, even if she cannot set it into words. The unfinished quality of the memory makes her more watchful, more ashamed, and more likely to interpret every argument, every sudden demand, every body of water, and every face that resembles her captors as a warning. That cycle has made her increasingly isolated at work and at home, and it was the growing impact on her sleep, her concentration at the pharmacy, and her relationship that finally brought her to seek help. What Amina says she wants most is to sleep without bracing for danger, but what frightens her most is that if she stops monitoring everything, the torture will return in full and she will not survive it a second time.
